query: The Widow's Game {Tonight's guest is a widow in black lace who has come up from the river towns to play cards with somebody young. She deals before you've sat down.|The widow is back, and asked for you by description: "the one who loses nicely."|The widow again. She has brought her own deck this time, and a flask she says is cough syrup.} The landlady murmurs: she tips the ones who make her laugh, and she always knows who's letting her win. Play her honestly, and well {You play your best and lose by a hair, and she laughs until she has to take her spectacles off. She tips you twice what you'd have won.|You beat her, once, and she's so pleased she tells you about her late husband's three duels. You go home at four, paid and full of stories.|You keep it close all night. When she leaves she pinches your cheek, presses a fold of notes on you, and says, "Next time, cheat a little. It's more fun."} {She sees through you in three hands, and is bored by the fourth. A small tip and an early night.|She plays you off the table, kindly, and tips like a woman who has won. It is not much.|You try too hard to amuse her. She pats your hand. "Never mind, dear," she says, and leaves early.} Let her win, gracefully {You lose with care all night. She knows, and tips you anyway, the way you'd tip a waiter for a bad soup.|You let her win. She thanks you very politely, which stings more than you expected.|You lose gracefully, as the landlady asked. The widow gives you exactly the going rate, and not a coin more.}
